evaluations.bottleneck: Before Long Short-Term Memory, learning long-range dependencies in recurrent networks was impractical because vanilla RNN gradients vanished or exploded over long sequences.

Before sequence-to-sequence learning, mapping an input sequence to an output sequence of different length with one end-to-end neural model was impractical because models required fixed-size inputs and task-specific alignment structure.

Q2.evidence: Sutskever et al. showed a single end-to-end LSTM encoder-decoder could translate whole sentences, framing translation and later tasks as generic sequence transduction that the Transformer directly inherited.
Q2.source: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
Q2.falsification: if the Transformer's encoder-decoder design were shown to derive independently of the seq2seq framing

Q6.evidence: Seq2seq supplied the deliberate design model of encoding a source sequence into a representation and decoding a target sequence from it, which is the macro-architecture of the original Transformer.
Q6.source: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
Q6.falsification: if the original Transformer had used a single-stack or non-encoder-decoder architecture

Q7.evidence: The encoder-decoder became the standard reusable interface for transduction tasks, implemented as a black-box pattern in frameworks and reused by the Transformer without change at that level.
Q7.source: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
Q7.falsification: if pre-Transformer systems had not standardized on encoder-decoder interfaces

Q11.evidence: The Transformer paper presents its model as a sequence transduction model following the encoder-decoder structure established by seq2seq work.
Q11.falsification: if the Transformer's lineage ran through a non-seq2seq task formulation instead

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Bahdanau attention, neural translation of long sentences was impractical because the decoder had to compress the entire source into one fixed-length vector.

Q1.evidence: Bahdanau et al. showed jointly learning to align and translate let the decoder use all source positions, sharply improving translation of long sentences that fixed-vector models degraded on.
Q1.source: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Q1.falsification: if fixed-vector encoder-decoders had matched attention on long sentences

Q2.evidence: Attention generalized from an alignment add-on into self-attention, the sole sequence-mixing operation of the Transformer, unlocking the entire architecture family built on it.
Q2.falsification: if the Transformer had retained recurrence or convolution as its primary sequence mixer

Q6.evidence: Bahdanau attention supplied the explanatory model of content-based soft alignment over source states that the Transformer authors generalized into query-key-value self-attention.
Q6.source: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
Q6.falsification: if self-attention were shown to derive from an unrelated mechanism with no alignment lineage

Q7.evidence: Attention became a standard composable module inserted into encoder-decoder models throughout 2015-2017 and then reused as the Transformer's core building block.
Q7.source: Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
Q7.falsification: if attention had remained a one-off component of a single translation system

Q11.evidence: The Transformer paper explicitly builds on attention mechanisms from Bahdanau-style neural machine translation and extends them to self-attention.
Q11.falsification: if removing the attention lineage left the Transformer's stated design history intact

Q12.evidence: After attention, sequence modeling did not return to fixed-vector bottlenecks, and attention remained the default mixing operation through the Transformer era.
Q12.falsification: if post-2017 mainstream sequence models had abandoned attention for fixed-vector encoding

evaluations.bottleneck: Before the Gated Recurrent Unit, gated recurrent sequence modeling required the heavier LSTM cell because simpler RNNs could not retain information over long spans.

Before ByteNet, non-recurrent sequence transduction at character level was impractical because available convolutional and recurrent designs could not preserve linear time and resolution over long byte sequences.
Before Word2vec embeddings, obtaining useful dense word representations cheaply was impractical because prior neural language-model embeddings were slow to train at vocabulary scale.
Before deep residual learning, training very deep networks was impractical because added layers degraded accuracy through optimization difficulty rather than overfitting.

Q2.evidence: Residual learning made networks of over 100 layers trainable, and the identity-shortcut pattern it unlocked is reused in every Transformer block to stack many layers.
Q2.source: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Q2.falsification: if deep Transformer stacks had trained equally well with plain non-residual layers

Q6.evidence: ResNet supplied the deliberate design model of learning residual functions with identity shortcuts, which the Transformer adopted verbatim as residual connections around each sub-layer.
Q6.falsification: if the Transformer's residual connections were shown to come from a different, independent design source

Q7.evidence: The residual block became a standard module used without regard to its internal optimization rationale, including in each Transformer encoder and decoder layer.
Q7.falsification: if residual connections had remained specific to ResNet-style vision networks

Q8.evidence: Residual connections spread from image recognition into sequence modeling and became a default element of deep architectures across vision and language.
Q8.falsification: if residual connections had stayed confined to image classification

Q10.evidence: Residual networks displaced plain deep networks as the default way to build very deep models after winning ILSVRC 2015 with a 152-layer network.
Q10.source: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Q10.falsification: if plain deep networks had remained the default after 2015

Q11.evidence: The Transformer paper specifies a residual connection around each of its sub-layers, placing ResNet's mechanism directly on the architecture's trunk line.
Q11.falsification: if the original Transformer had contained no residual connections

Q12.evidence: Deep architectures after ResNet, including all mainstream Transformers, retained identity shortcuts rather than returning to plain stacked layers.
Q12.source: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
Q12.falsification: if later deep models had abandoned residual connections as a default

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Layer Normalization, normalizing recurrent and sequence networks was impractical because batch statistics depended on sequence length and batch composition.

Q2.evidence: Layer normalization made per-example normalization work for sequence models, and the Transformer embeds it in every sub-layer, enabling its deep stacks to train stably.
Q2.falsification: if the original Transformer had trained to its reported results using batch normalization or no normalization

Q7.evidence: LayerNorm became a standard off-the-shelf module in sequence architectures, applied in the Transformer as 'Add & Norm' after every sub-layer without users reasoning about its statistics.
Q7.falsification: if LayerNorm had not been adopted as a reusable component beyond its original paper

Q11.evidence: The Transformer architecture diagram and text specify layer normalization following each residual sub-layer connection, making it part of the original design.
Q11.falsification: if layer normalization were absent from the original Transformer specification

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Dropout, regularizing large neural networks against co-adaptation was impractical because ensemble averaging over subnetworks was too expensive to perform directly.
Before GloVe, deriving word vectors that combined global corpus statistics with local context was impractical because count-based and predictive methods each captured only part of that structure.

Before cross-entropy loss, scoring a predicted distribution against observed outcomes lacked a principled differentiable objective because there was no standard measure of mismatch between probability distributions.
Before gradient descent, systematically minimizing a differentiable function was impractical because there was no general iterative rule that followed the direction of steepest decrease.

Before Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation, computing exact derivatives of composite numerical programs efficiently was impractical because symbolic differentiation blew up and finite differences were inaccurate and costly.
Before backpropagation, training multilayer neural networks was impractical because there was no efficient general method for assigning credit to hidden units.

Q2.evidence: Backpropagation made training arbitrary multilayer networks feasible, unlocking the entire deep-learning program of which the Transformer is one architecture.
Q2.falsification: if multilayer networks including Transformers had been trainable at scale by a comparably general non-gradient method

Q3.evidence: No ready substitute in 1986 or in 2017 could train deep networks with millions of parameters as generally as backpropagation, and the Transformer was trained with it via Adam.
Q3.falsification: if the original Transformer had been trained by a method not based on backpropagated gradients

Q6.evidence: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams supplied the chain-rule credit-assignment model that made deliberate design and training of deep architectures, including the Transformer, possible.
Q6.falsification: if deep network training had proceeded without a gradient-based credit-assignment model

Q8.evidence: Backpropagation underlies trained models across vision, speech, language and control, far beyond the perceptron settings in which it was popularized.
Q8.falsification: if backpropagation had remained confined to small demonstration networks

Q9.evidence: Reverse-mode gradient computation costs a small constant multiple of a forward pass regardless of parameter count, collapsing gradient estimation versus per-parameter numerical differentiation by orders of magnitude.
Q9.falsification: if numerical differentiation had been comparably cheap for million-parameter networks

Q11.evidence: Every parameter of the original Transformer was learned by backpropagation-based optimization, so removing it breaks the model's actual training history.
Q11.falsification: if the Transformer had been constructed or fitted without gradient training

Q12.evidence: Gradient-based training via backpropagation remained the universal default for neural networks through and beyond the Transformer era.
Q12.falsification: if the field had reverted to hand-designed or non-gradient-trained networks

evaluations.bottleneck: Before A Mathematical Theory of Communication, information had no quantitative definition because communication was described qualitatively without a unit or measure of uncertainty.

Q5.evidence: Shannon defined entropy in bits, making the information content of a source a measurable quantity that later underlies cross-entropy training objectives.
Q5.falsification: if entropy had not provided a usable quantitative measure adopted by later work

evaluations.bottleneck: Before CUDA, programming GPUs for general computation was impractical because developers had to disguise computation as graphics operations through graphics APIs.

Q4.evidence: CUDA exposed GPU throughput to general code, and GPU training of neural networks delivered order-of-magnitude speedups over CPUs in the deep-learning era preceding the Transformer.
Q4.falsification: if GPU training under CUDA had offered only marginal speedups over contemporary CPUs

Q9.evidence: GPU acceleration cut neural network training runs from weeks to days in the pre-Transformer deep-learning literature, directly shortening experiment cycles.
Q9.source: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
Q9.falsification: if CUDA-based training had not materially shortened training times

evaluations.bottleneck: Before TensorFlow, deploying and scaling dataflow-based machine learning across machines was impractical for most teams because prior systems were research-bound or hard to productionize.
Before ImageNet, training and benchmarking visual recognition at scale was impractical because existing labeled image datasets were orders of magnitude too small.
Before the WMT workshop, comparing machine translation systems systematically was impractical because there was no recurring shared task with common data and evaluation.
Before the BLEU score, evaluating machine translation output was slow and expensive because quality assessment depended on repeated human judgment for every system change.

Q5.evidence: BLEU made translation quality automatically measurable via n-gram precision against references, and the Transformer paper reported its headline results as BLEU scores on WMT tasks.
Q5.source: BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation
Q5.falsification: if the Transformer's results had not been stated or compared in BLEU

Q7.evidence: BLEU became the standard reporting interface for machine translation systems, used by the Transformer paper to claim state-of-the-art results comparable across prior work.
Q7.falsification: if BLEU had not been the common metric in the results tables the Transformer compared against
